newsitem.title: HUNGARY: Analysts see limits to Hungary stocks growth.
newsitem.headline: Analysts see limits to Hungary stocks growth.

text.p: The Budapest Stock Exchange (BSE) has used up most of its growth potential for the year with an 81 percent rise in forint terms since January, analysts said on Tuesday.
"We think, frankly, that most of the rises happened for the whole year," said Andrew Thomson, head of European Emerging Markets Research at Dresdner Kleinwort Benson in London.

The BUX index of the BSE, which was among the top performers globally in 1996, peaked at 7,491.07 points on July 17, rising 3,356.76 points or 81.2 percent since the 1996-end level of 4,134.31 points.
On Tuesday the BUX index closed at 7,439.09.
Frances Cloud, analyst at Nomura Equity Research in London, said she did not expect more than a 10 percent gain in the BUX index by the end of 1997.

"On fundamentals it ought not to go up, it ought to go down, but in reality it probably will continue to go up," she said. "But I tend to set a maximum increase of 10 percent which is effectively the rate of inflation in the second half of the year," she added.
Hungary expects to push average inflation down to about 18 percent this year from 23.6 percent in 1996. In June, year-on-year inflation was 18.7 percent.
Market participants saw several factors behind the market's recent bull run, such as improving macroeconomy, good corporate earnings growth and a stable political base.

The fact that funds were directed to Hungary from the Czech Republic and Poland due to economic problems and floods there, and the recent strong dollar also contributed to the Budapest bourse's strength, they added.

However, some market participants say the rise is also linked to the market's relatively tight liquidity, with investors having to pay a higher price if they want to acquire substantial amounts of shares.
Cloud said that all the major Hungarian stocks were fully valued in the light of their expected earnings and some of them were overvalued.
"(Home-improvement-product maker) Graboplast or even (pharmaceutical firm) Richter are now more expensive than similar companies in Western Europe," she said.

Graboplast on Tuesday rallied to a new high of 11,600 forints, before it gave up some of its gains to end at 11,400, up 440. Richter also jumped to a new high of 18,200 forints on Tuesday, before retreating to close at 18,100.

Thomson said that earnings growth of Hungarian companies would probably be better in the first half of 1997 than in the second half of the year and this would translate into less buoyancy on the market by the end of the year.
